issue_context.title: Improve `formatting` docs
issue_context.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

From @vilmibm's [comment](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/6089#issuecomment-1226075409) I'd like to try and improve the output of the `gh help formatting` command. `jq` filters and `go` templates are very powerful, however the syntax and problems they solve can be confusing to newcomers, especially if they have less experience with the command line.

### Proposed solution

Goals:
- [ ] Add more context on `--json`, `--jq`, and `--template` flags
- [ ] Explain the problems they each can solve
- [ ] Add more detailed examples
- [ ] Be accessible, not overwhelming

### Additional context

I was wondering if the `formatting` help command https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/9aafd0da1344e611f3e49c74a043d6a25b460d0a/pkg/cmd/root/help_topic.go#L91 might be split into subcommands for each of `--json`, `--jq`, and `--template`, and have the root `formatting` command reference the subcommands. For example:
```
$ gh help formatting

Optional flags to further format the string based output of a command. For more information, see
* gh help formatting json
* gh help formatting jq
* gh help formatting template
```
This isn't necessary but I do think it would make the content easier to view and contextualize if it is separated into pieces. It would also allow the example sections to be specific to argument.

I was also wondering if there are any additional steps to preview the output of the command in html to ensure it looks correct in https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_formatting
comments:
Thanks for taking this on!! 🚀 

> I was wondering if the `formatting` help command might be split into subcommands 

I'm not sure if this is useful right now. Both `--jq` and `--template` only make sense combined with the `--json` flag, so to document it on separate man pages might be counter-productive. Also, if all these topics are split into subtopics, then `gh help formatting` output itself will not produce anything useful other thank links to other pages.

> I was also wondering if there are any additional steps to preview the output of the command in html to ensure it looks correct

You can invoke `./cmd/gen-docs` to generate Markdown files for a Jekyll site: https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/465b952d85404e52bea5537d12f914071b2eff5d/Makefile#L44

However, the final Jekyll transformation isn't available for you to preview because our documentation site isn't a public repo. My advice would be to just inspect the generated Markdown.

review_comments:
I've missed this in my original review: “according to a required formatting string” doesn't sound right to me. When using `--json`, passing a formatting string isn't required at all. Also, “formatting according to … formatting string” sound repetitive. How about:

> Once in JSON, the output can be further formatted using either `--jq` or `--template` flag.

Ah, I think I understand now. You have been using the pattern “the `--foo` flag _requires_ so and so value”, which reads odd to me because I haven't seen this phrasing before, but it is technically correct that all of these flags require a value. Only boolean flags do not need a value.

Elsewhere, I think we've been using “the `--foo` flag _accepts_ so and so value”, which reads a bit softer than “requires”, but ultimately there are no hard and fast rules around this.

This `--template` example outputs the exact format of regular `gh pr list`, which isn't very compelling as an example for using `--template`. How about changing something about this expression so that the final output is somehow different (and potentially more useful to some people) than regular `gh pr list`?

I wondered about that. I think this is more helpful because it's already known, and you can see how to sort of reverse engineer it using templates. I personally find a small tweak or revealing how something is done is easier for me to pattern match against. What do you think?

Well, it can stay like this if the goal was to demonstrate how one can reverse-engineer the default output. But, from the user's perspective, they might be scanning these examples and seeing how one simple `gh` invocation and one seemingly very complicated `gh` invocation both produce the same result.

I'll leave the final decision up to you. The example itself is indeed useful as a starting point for editing one's template.

I included example output from each of the example commands so users can view them and compare without needing to run the commands, which could be helpful in the web view. The downside is it's not consistent with other examples, and a lot more verbose which may be distracting, and risks getting out of date at some point in the future. 

Leaving it in for discussion but it can definitely be removed
